entries.title: Grammar: Ezafe chains
entries.body: The unstressed suffix _-e_ (or _-ye_ after vowels) links head noun to modifiers in sequence. Long chains stack as **head – modifier – modifier – modifier**. Written text usually leaves the ezafe unwritten except on words ending in silent `ه` (→ `ۀ`) or `ی` (→ `یِ`).

examples.en: the tender mercies of the Lord.
a pillar of fire. [here `az` introduces the material, not ezafe — contrast with ezafe-linked modifiers]

etym.prose: transliteration of English _Nephi_, the Book of Mormon prophet's name. Sometimes connected to Egyptian _nfr_ "good, fair" or to Hebrew, but Persian here just spells the English form phonetically.
`فرمان` + `روا` (← `رفتن`) + `-ی` ([abstract suffix](../word_formation.html#the-abstract-noun-suffix-g)) → "having one's commands run/effected".

entries.family: `فرمان` _farmān_ "command, decree"; `روا` _ravā_ "current, permitted" (also an entry in this chapter); `فرمانروا` _farmān-ravā_ "ruler, sovereign".

entries.title: Grammar: Possessive / pronominal suffixes
entries.body: Attached directly to nouns: _-am_ (my), _-at_ (thy), _-aš_ (his/her/its), _-mān_ (our), _-tān_ (your), _-šān_ (their). Persian usually prefers these clitics to the full-pronoun + ezafe construction (`کتاب من` "my book" → `کتابم`).

examples.persian: من، نیفای، از پدر و مادر{e} خوبی زاده شده
examples.translit: man, Nīfāy, az pedar o mādar-e xūb-ī zāde šode

examples.persian: نگاشته ای از کارهایم در روزگارم را می‌نگارم
examples.translit: negāšte-ī az kārhā-yam dar rūzgār-am-rā mī-negāram
examples.en: I write an account of my works in my days. [`-am` on `kārhā` and on `rūzgār`; `-rā` marks the whole phrase as direct object of `می‌نگارم`]

entries.closing: Watch especially for _-aš_ in third-person narrative: _پدرش pedar-aš_, _روزگارش rūzgār-aš_, _جانش jān-aš_, _دلش del-aš_, _روانش ravān-aš_, _مردمش mardom-aš_.

etym.prose: Persian transliteration of English _Sariah_; sometimes equated with Hebrew _Sāray_/_Sārā_ "princess".

entries.title: Grammar: Relative clauses with `که`
entries.body: `که` introduces both complement clauses ("that he …") and relative clauses ("who, which, that"). For relatives the head noun usually carries indefinite _-ī_, i.e. `X-ī ke …` = "an X which …". The verb inside the relative clause is in whatever tense fits the sense.

examples.persian: به سبب{e} چیزهایی که دید و شنید
examples.translit: be sabab-e čīzhā-yī ke dīd o šenīd
examples.en: because of the things which he had seen and heard.

entries.closing: Note how `چیز + ها + ی + ی` stacks: plural `-hā` + ezafe `-ye` (invisible in writing) + indefinite `-ī` → `čīzhā-yī`, then `که` introduces the relative.

from Arabic, comparative form of _rāšid_ "rightly-guided", root r-š-d "to be on the right path".

entries.title: Grammar: Imperfective `می-` and its negation `نمی-`
entries.body:
The prefix _mī-_ marks non-perfective aspect — present-tense, habitual, or past-progressive readings depending on the stem:

- Present stem + _mī-_ + endings → present (`می‌نگارم` = "I write / I am writing").
- Past stem + _mī-_ + endings → past habitual/continuous (`می‌کرد` = "he used to do / was doing").

Negation fuses: `نمی‌نگارم` ("I do not write"), `نمی‌کرد` ("he was not doing"). Watch out: in compound verbs the _mī-_ attaches only to the auxiliary: `نبوّت می‌کند`, `گواهی می‌داد`.

examples.persian: و اینک من، نیفای، سرگذشت{e} کاملی از چیزهایی که پدرم نوشته است نمی‌نگارم
examples.translit: va īnak man, Nīfāy, sargozašt-e kāmel-ī az čīzhā-yī ke pedar-am nevešte ast nemī-negāram
examples.en: And now I, Nephi, do not write a full account of the things which my father has written.

entries.title: Grammar: Passive voice with `شدن`
entries.body: Persian forms the passive with `[past participle] + شدن` (conjugated). The agent, if named, is introduced with `از سوی` ("by the hand of") — there's a classic example in verse 7.

examples.persian: از سوی{e} یهودیان آزار داده می‌شود
examples.translit: az sūy-e Yahūdiyān āzār dāde mī-šavad
examples.en: He is persecuted by the Jews.

entries.closing: Another (future passive), [verse 13](#verse-13): `ساکنان آن نابود خواهند شد ... بسیاری با شمشیر هلاک خواهند شد، و بسیاری به اسارت به بابل برده خواهند شد` — the inhabitants will be destroyed, many will perish by the sword, and many will be carried captive to Babylon.

entries.family: `سر` _sar_ "head" (an entry in this chapter); [`-ور`](../word_formation.html#var-possessing-bearing-x) _-var_ (productive suffix; cf. `هنرور` "skilled", `کینه‌ور` "vengeful").

the unmarked spelling `سرور` is the citation form

entries.title: Grammar: Archaic / biblical register
entries.body:
The translation deliberately uses a high-register Persian that mirrors the KJV-style English of the original. Things to recognize:

- `گفتا` (_goftā_) — archaic narrative past of `گفتن`, roughly "said he" (the `-ā` is a narrative ending in classical Persian).
- `آری` (_ārī_) — "yea, indeed," peppered throughout; literary equivalent of `بله`.
- `بنگرید` (_benegarīd_) — "behold!" (2pl imperative of `نگریستن`).
- `سرور` (_Sarvar_) — the translator's word for "the Lord"; in ordinary Persian it means "master, chief." Vocative `سرورا` ([verse 14](#verse-14), "O Lord!") uses the classical `-ā` vocative.
- Bookish verbs chosen over everyday equivalents: `نگاشتن` for `نوشتن` (write), `نیایش کردن` for `دعا کردن` (pray), `بانگ برآوردن` for `فریاد زدن` (cry out), `نمودن` for `کردن`/`نشان دادن`.

examples.persian: او خواند، گفتا: وای، وای بر اورشلیم
examples.translit: ū xānd, goftā: vāy, vāy bar Uršalīm
examples.en: And he read, saying: Woe, woe unto Jerusalem.

etym.prose: native Persian compound, traditionally analyzed as `هش` (← `هوش`) + `دار` (← `داشتن`) "alert-holding".

entries.family: `هوش` _hūš_ "consciousness, alertness, intelligence"; `داشتن` _dāštan_ "to hold" (an entry in this chapter); `هوشیار` _hūšyār_ "vigilant".

forms.desc: 3sg pres. _`می دهد` mī-dehad_, as in `هشدار می دهد` "warns / gives warning"
pp. _`داده` dāde_. The pres stem `deh-` always carries `می-` (indicative) or `بـ-` (subjunctive) in modern Persian
bare `دهد` is classical/literary or a compound-verb subjunctive with the `بـ-` dropped

entries.title: Grammar: Subjunctive after `تا`
entries.body: `تا` + subjunctive marks purpose ("so that"). The subjunctive is formed with the present stem + personal endings, with the بـ- prefix for simple verbs (`بخواند`), but **without بـ- for compound verbs** (`توانا سازد`, not `*توانا بسازد`). This بـ- drop in compound verbs is systematic across all light verbs (`کردن`, `شدن`, `دادن`, `ساختن`, …) and is the norm in formal/literary Persian — the register this translation uses throughout. In colloquial Persian the بـ- is usually kept, so `توانا بسازد` sounds natural in everyday speech.

examples.persian: از او خواست تا آن را بخواند
examples.translit: az ū xāst tā ān-rā bexānad
examples.en: He asked him to read it ("so that he might read it").

examples.persian: تا آنها را ... به قدرت{e} رهایی توانا سازد
examples.translit: tā ānhā-rā … be qodrat-e rahāyī tavānā sāzad
examples.en: that he may enable them … by the power of deliverance.

[`نا-`](../word_formation.html#n-un-non-in) + [`بکار`](../word_formation.html#be-in-with-by) ([به‌-](../word_formation.html#be-in-with-by) + `کار` "work") + `-ی` ([abstract suffix](../word_formation.html#the-abstract-noun-suffix-g)) → "non-useful-ness, wickedness".

entries.title: Grammar: Compound verbs (light-verb constructions)
entries.body: Persian builds most of its verbs as **noun/adjective + کردن / شدن / زدن / دادن / …**. The "meaning" lives in the non-verbal element; the light verb handles inflection. Examples from this chapter: `نبوّت کردن` (to prophesy), `ستایش کردن` (to praise), `توبه کردن` (to repent), `نیایش کردن` (to pray), `گواهی دادن` (to testify), `نشان دادن` (to show), `نابود شدن` (to be destroyed), `چیره شدن` (to be overcome), `پیش رفتن` (to go forth), `تکان خوردن` (to be shaken), `بانگ برآوردن` (to raise a cry).

examples.en: He foretells the coming of Christ.

entries.title: Grammar: Direct-object marker `را`
entries.body: `را` clitic marks a **specific/definite** direct object. It attaches to the **end of the whole object phrase**, not to the head noun — so it often sits after relative clauses, adjectives, or even coordinated phrases.

examples.persian: نیفای نگاشتۀ مردمش را شروع می‌نماید
examples.en: Nephi begins the account of his people. [`-rā` marks the whole phrase `نگاشتۀ مردمش`]

entries.closing: Also compare, within [verse 3](#verse-3): `این نگاشته ای که می‌نگارم راست است` (no `را`, because it's a predicate) with `من آن را با دست خودم می‌نگارم` (`را` marks the definite direct object `آن`).

entries.title: Grammar: `چنین گذشت` — "and it came to pass"
entries.body: A Hebrew/biblical calque that opens many verses. Structurally it's `čonīn` ("thus") + past of `gozaštan` ("to pass"). Treat it as a fixed idiom; don't try to unpack "thus passed" mechanically.

examples.persian: زیرا چنین گذشت در آغاز{e} نخستین سال{e} فرمانروایی{e} صدقیا، پادشاه{e} یهودا

entries.title: Grammar: Indefinite `-ī`
entries.body: The suffix _-ī_ attached to a noun marks "a, a certain, one" (similar to English _a/an_). Don't confuse it with the _-ī_ that makes adjectives abstract-nouns (`خوب` "good" → `خوبی` "goodness") — context usually disambiguates.

examples.persian: از پدر و مادر{e} خوبی زاده شده
examples.translit: az pedar o mādar-e xūb-ī zāde šode

entries.title: Grammar: Future tense: `خواه- + short infinitive`
entries.body: Formed with the present of `خواستن` (_xāh-am, xāh-ī, xāh-ad, xāh-īm, xāh-īd, xāh-and_) plus the **short infinitive** (past stem; `نگاشتن → نگاشت`, `شدن → شد`, `بردن → برد`). Negation: `نخواهم نگاشت` etc. Note the short infinitive does **not** take endings — all person/number marking is on the auxiliary.

intro:
## Intro
The source text has three layers: (1) a **book-level summary** of all of 1 Nephi, which previews Lehi's whole story — Sariah, the four sons, the journey into the wilderness, Ishmael's daughters, the ship, the promised land — and is therefore full of vocabulary you won't meet again for many chapters; (2) a short **chapter heading** summarizing chapter 1 itself; and (3) the **20 verses** of chapter 1 proper. Content-wise, chapter 1 is Nephi introducing himself, describing his father Lehi's vision of a pillar of fire and book of prophecy, Jerusalem's coming destruction, and the Jews' mockery and threats; Nephi closes by saying the Lord (Sarvar) delivers those with faith.

Each section below opens with the Persian text from the source, immediately followed by the vocabulary it introduces. The **book summary** is broken out **sentence-by-sentence**, while the **chapter summary** and the **verses** each have their own vocab section.
vocab_intro: Organized in **order of first appearance**, grouped by verse. A word appears in the verse where you first encounter it; inflected forms of a verb already introduced (e.g. a new past-tense of a verb you saw earlier) are not re-listed. Proper nouns are mixed in where they first appear, tagged `[proper]`. Verbs include infinitive and present stem.
book_summary_intro: The pre-chapter heading for the whole First Book of Nephi. Many of these lemmas preview vocabulary for later chapters (ship, wilderness, brothers, promised land).
closing: The chapter packs many of the constructions you'll meet repeatedly: the `چنین گذشت` opener, `شدن`-passives, ezafe chains, compound verbs with `کردن`/`شدن`, object-marker `را` riding on long noun phrases, and relative `که`-clauses. Once those click, the vocabulary starts to do most of the work. Read verse-by-verse, resist reaching for the translation until you've parsed the Persian yourself, and keep this guide open to the vocab page — most of chapter 2 will reuse ~60% of it.
